messages.subject: command options & adaptation for Metropolis
parts:
Peter's got the basic Metropolis working end to end, so
it's time to think about adaptation and configuration.

1. How do we want Metropolis to be configurable?
At very least, I'm imagining:

-- adapted single step size * unit covariance

-- adapted diagonal covariance matrix

-- adapted full covariance matrix

Do we need to include user-specified step sizes and user-specified
covar matrices in addition?

If so, any suggestions on how to set up the classes?
Specifically, do we have three classes,

metropolis_unit_covar
metropolis_diag_covar
metropolis_full_covar

that let us configure adaptation vs. user input, or six
classes, the above plus user-specified matrix versions?

2. How should we be doing adaptation for Metropolis?

Does it make sense to independently adapt a global
scale (step size in HMC) and a standardized
covariance matrix (inverse mass matrix in HMC)?
We can't just let both be free due to identifiability
issues, right?

Here's what I'm imagining:

- parameters: scale epsilon, standardized covariance Sigma_std;
proposal covariance matrix: Sigma = epsilon * Sigma_std

- initialize covariance matrix Sigma to unit diagonal

- find a scale epsilon that gives us roughly 23.4% acceptance rates
[or make acceptance rate target configurable]

- run warmup iterations after 100 (200, 400, ...) iterations:
+ use last half of iterations' acceptance rate to adjust
epsilon up or down
+ use last half of iterations to estimate standardized
covariance matrix (???)

How do we standardize the covariance matrix estimate?

- Bob

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] command options & adaptation for Metropolis
parts:
It depends on how fancy we want things to get. I think a basic
version which estimates a covariance matrix given the previous samples
(full, diagonal or scaled identity) and then uses a mixture proposal
which uses the rescaled (see
http://probability.ca/jeff/ftpdir/galinart.pdf) estimated covariance
most of the time and sometimes uses a conservative proposal to avoid
excess sticking would be good. Other possibilities are to use a
mixtures of multivariate Student T distributions which takes into
account the uncertainty in estimating the covariance matrix. User
visible parameters would then be things like probability of using
adapted covariance, whether to use student t or gaussian proposals,
etc.

Also, there isn't really a stepsize in Metropolis, that's just an HMC
thing, so no, I don't think it really makes sense to adapt a global
scale separately.

Cheers,
Marcus

I was picturing a complete analogy to the HMC code,

metro_unit_covar
metro_diag_covar
metro_dense_covar

and then use multiple inheritance with the above and the adaptive sampler to yield

adapt_metro_unit_covar
adapt_metro_diag_covar
adapt_metro_dense_covar

> 2. How should we be doing adaptation for Metropolis?
>
> Does it make sense to independently adapt a global
> scale (step size in HMC) and a standardized
> covariance matrix (inverse mass matrix in HMC)?
> We can't just let both be free due to identifiability
> issues, right?

>
> - parameters: scale epsilon, standardized covariance Sigma_std;
> proposal covariance matrix: Sigma = epsilon * Sigma_std
>
> - initialize covariance matrix Sigma to unit diagonal
>
> - find a scale epsilon that gives us roughly 23.4% acceptance rates
> [or make acceptance rate target configurable]
>
> - run warmup iterations after 100 (200, 400, ...) iterations:
> + use last half of iterations' acceptance rate to adjust
> epsilon up or down
> + use last half of iterations to estimate standardized
> covariance matrix (???)
>
> How do we standardize the covariance matrix estimate?

I don't think there will be identifiability issues here. You have d(d -1) / 2 correlations for estimating the covariance and the Metropolis acceptance rate for estimating the step size. Remember that the optimal scaling in Metropolis is not the covariance but some scaling of the covariance that depends on dimension (at least in IID gaussian models, etc). Having a free step size will avoid our having to determine that a priori.

Again, I think we can reuse all the HMC code (which is why the reusable parts are in mcmc and not mcmc/hmc!).

1) Initialize covariance matrix to unit diagonal - the regularized estimator takes care of this for us.

2) Initialize stepsize to about 0.234 - 0.5 should be close enough for an initial guess. Which means we can copy the init_stepsize code in HMC only using propose instead of evolve.

3) We should be able to adapt the step size as we go and then update the covariance after the usual windows.

How do we adapt the step size as we go? It looks like what
it's doing now is calling the equivalent of find_reasonable_stepsize()

in half repeatedly based on proposals (from an initial position or
what -- here's where the code loses me?).

(Aside question: wouldn't a finer-grained factor like
like sqrt(2) or sqrt(sqrt(2)) be better? Adaptation is slower
by a factor of 2 or 4, but we'd get closer
than to within a factor of 2 of the "right" answer.)

I think I understand the covar matrix estimation, but let
me make sure. At intervals during warmup (say after 100,
after 200, after 400 iterations, etc.), we'll take the
second half of the iterations (so after 100, we'd take
iterations 51--100, after 200 we take iterations 101-200) and
use the "sampled" parameter values to estimate a covariance matrix.
We can do this in a fixed amount of memory and reasonable numerical
stability with Welford's algorithm.

Until we get to the end. If someone specifieds 875 warmup
iterations, then what do we do? We'll have buffered
400--800, then we'll start again, but don't just want to use
the last 75. And this'll be a huge mess in the time-based
approach when we don't even know how many warmup iterations
we'll get.

Also, someone mentioned only using the warmup iterations that
were not Metropolis rejected. Should we do that?

- Bob

> what -- here's where the code loses me?).

Init_stepsize is called only after --the (co)variance is updated--, not at every iteration. The problem is that when you update the (co)variance the optimal step size changes, and initializing the step size again avoids unnecessary burden on the dual-averaging (remember we're not using a "standardized" metric anymore).

> like sqrt(2) or sqrt(sqrt(2)) be better? Adaptation is slower

Yeah. In fact, I think I've seen behavior to this effect already (it shows up as unoptimal acceptance rates in the final samples).
Should we not make the windows arbitrary but scale them to the total number of warm-up iterations? i.e. assume five windows and just take the first window to be of size (warm-up iterations) / 2^{5}, second window (warm-up) iterations) / 2^{4}, etc.

I was.

Here's the issue in detail. You've defined the constructor as

adapt_dense_metro(M &m, BaseRNG& rng, std::ostream* error_msg)
: dense_metro<M, BaseRNG>(m, rng, this->_propCov, error_msg),
stepsize_covar_adapter(m.num_params_r())
{
this->_propCov.resize(m.num_params_r(), m.num_params_r());
this->_propCov.setIdentity();
};

When you try to construct adapt_dense_metro multiple constructors are called, from base to derived. So in this case you call

base_mcmc()
base_metro()
dense_metro<M, BaseRNG>(m, rng, this->_propCov, error_msg)

base_adapter()
stepsize_covar_adapter(m.num_params_r())

and then finally

{
this->_propCov.resize(m.num_params_r(), m.num_params_r());
this->_propCov.setIdentity();
};
Let's focus on the dense_metro constructor,
dense_metro<M, BaseRNG>(m, rng, this->_propCov, error_msg)

You've given this->_propCov as an argument, but it doesn't exist yet! It only gets created once the arguments have been passed and the constructor executes. It's like writing

double x = x;

I'm not sure what the spec says, but I wouldn't be surprised if it gives undefined behavior which would explain why Ben and I see different results than you.

The error before was that I was passing a square matrix in for the mu argument, which should've only been a vector.

> this->_nom_epsilon = 1;
> }

>

>> {
>> this->_prop_cov.resize(m.num_params_r(), m.num_params_r());
>> this->_prop_cov.setIdentity();
>> };

>>
>>
>> Peter
>>

a double and template it out so it matches int better

To be precise, any extra samples wouldn't have affected anything because the (co)variance is updated only when a window closes, not when it opens. In any case, I updated the adapters to take in the total number of adaptation iterations (just the number of warm up samples in our case) and then snap the final adaptation window to the total warmup window so that no samples are wasted.

It should be straightforward to make this work with time-based approaches, as well, if we can assume constant samples/time.

The idea would be to estimate samples/time in vivo. So instead of sampling until you hit the max time, like

sample
if(time > max_time) break

you would time each sample, use that to estimate the number of samples remaining in the given time window, and then set the total number of samples to equal to the samples already run plus those estimated to be remaining.

start clock
sample
stop clock
sample_per_time = (n * sample_per_time + 1 / (delta t) ) / ( n + 1)
samples_remaining = remaining_time * sample_per_time
n_samples = n + samples_remaining

The final timing would be less accurate, but you get to have both features. There might be easier ways to accomplish this.

>
> I'd think it'd be easy to add to Welford's algorithm by adjusting

Technically that's not hard to do.  I think the problem with a moving average is that it can still be too sensitive to the past.  In particular, convergence of the Markov chain (and, perhaps more importantly, the disparity in values between unconverted and converged) can often outpace the forgetfulness of the moving average estimator.  Isn't that why we went to sequential windows in the first place?
